title: o at the end says /oh/
kidTitle: Meet the o on the end
parentNote: Yesterday it was e; today it is o, and the rule is word for word the same. When a word ends in o and there is nothing after it, the o says its own name — go, no, so, hello, hippo. The slip to expect is exactly yesterday's slip in a new coat: go read as gog, or no read to rhyme with not, because for eighty days an o in a word has meant the short one. The test is still what comes after. In got and not and hop there is a letter after the o, so it stays short. In go and no and so the word stops, and a stopping o says oh. Say the pairs out loud — got and go, not and no, sob and so — and let them hear the word fall off the end. It is worth pointing out that this works in long words too: hippo and banjo and mango all stop at an o, and every one of them says oh.

activities.mouthCue: Push your lips out into a small round ring, like blowing out a candle: oh.
activities.prompt: The same trick as yesterday, with a different letter. On the end of a word, o says its own name.

Two beats, and it still stops at the o. That is why the end says oh.
The long one. Run a finger under it, and do not stop until the o.
Three words that start with a g. Only one of them stops at the o.
The same again with an n. Two of these keep going after the o.

activities.title: The hippo that did not go
activities.prompt: Read the story one line at a time. Tap any word you want to hear again.
lines: A big hippo did sit in the road and did not want to go.
Dad did honk. The hippo did not go.
Meg did shout at it to go. The hippo did not go.
I did get out and did creep up to it and did tell it hello.
It did blink at me. It is hot, the road is hot, and so it did stop.
Then Mum did get the banjo and did sit up on the van.
She did strum a tune, and the hippo did lift up its chin.
He did tap out the tempo, and we did clap and sing.
The hippo did stand up and did stomp off up the road in tempo.
No honk did shift it and no shout did shift it. A tune did.
